name: Omar Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the customer line for a parcel delivery firm, at the regional hub out by the ring road. People ring when a parcel's gone missing, been left in the rain, or the driver says they weren't home when they were. I track it, check the driver's photo, and either rebook it or start a claim. My desk looks down onto the loading bays, so I can watch the vans going out all morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are you getting on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: About a year. My manager says I'm too slow on claims because I check every detail, and my scores are near the bottom. We've got an AI tool that reads the tracking history and writes a summary, and I use it when the queue is long, though I always check it. I live with my partner Leila, who's a school receptionist, and we're saving to get married, but there's less than a month's money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first of five pictures of the future. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. I can believe that, to be honest. Half the things they promise never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought, it's a useful tool and nothing more. At work I'd say a parcel still needs a person when it goes wrong. I don't post much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's probably safe in that one, parcels go missing every day. What worries me is my scores and my pay, which is lower than the drivers get. And there aren't many office jobs round here if I lost this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get faster on claims, using the summary tool on every call, not just busy ones. I'd ask about a forklift licence the depot pays for, because the warehouse pays better on nights. And Leila and I would keep putting sixty a month into the wedding pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit frustrated about being stuck at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at the warehouse if your job is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the warehouse lads earn more than me on nights, and you can see what you've done at the end of a shift. My dad was a forklift driver for twenty years. It's honest work and it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would sixty a month mean for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much on its own, but it adds up. We want a small wedding with family and the mosque hall, nothing flash. I won't borrow for a wedding, that's how I was raised.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd say a parcel still needs **a person** when it goes wrong.
think: His job is **probably safe**, since parcels go missing every day.
His **scores and pay** worry him more, with few office jobs nearby.
do: Use the **summary tool** on every call to speed up claims.
Ask about the depot-funded **forklift licence** for better night pay.
Keep saving **sixty a month** for the wedding.
feel: **Okay** mostly, but **frustrated** at being stuck at the bottom.
S0.quote: I won't borrow for a wedding, that's how I was raised.
fieldNote: He sees the **warehouse** as better paid and more honest work.
He uses the AI tool, but **always checks** it.
His refusal to **borrow** reflects his traditional values.

steps.text: Use the tracking summary tool on every claims call
Ask the depot about its funded forklift licence
Put sixty a month into the wedding pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers is the first thing on the list. That's my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the company's right to run things how they want, but they should look after the people who've been loyal. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get a licence or a trade. I'd say the same at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the customer line shrinks a lot. Tracking and rebooking is exactly what a computer does well, and I'm slow. The warehouse and the vans would last longer, because robots come slower to hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence in the first few months, once I'd seen it worked for a couple of the lads. Then I'd ask for a transfer to nights in the warehouse. Leila and I would push the wedding back six months so we've got a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see it work for others first. How long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not long, a couple of months. Two lads from the customer line already moved down to the warehouse last spring. If they're doing well, I'll follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Leila feel about pushing the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd understand, she's sensible. But her mother would ask questions. I'd rather explain a delay than start married life in debt.

say: I'd say firms have **the right** to change, but should look after **loyal staff**.
I'd tell younger colleagues to get **a licence** or a trade.
think: The customer line **shrinks**, as tracking and rebooking suit a computer.
The **warehouse** lasts longer because robots arrive later.
do: Get the **forklift licence** in the first few months.
Ask for a **transfer to nights** in the warehouse.
Push the **wedding back** six months to build a buffer.
feel: **Uneasy**, but he can see **a way through**.

fieldNote: He follows **two colleagues** who already moved to the warehouse.
He defends the **company's right** to automate while asking for loyalty in return.
The **wedding delay** is a practical, not emotional, decision for him.

steps.text: Get the forklift licence within the first few months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to keep their heads and look after their families. I wouldn't be asking the government for handouts. I'd say get any hands-on work you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk job is gone almost straight away. The warehouse would last until robots in 2031, but everyone from every office would be trying to get in. So I'd need to move fast, not wait for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the forklift licence that month, not wait, and beg for nights in the warehouse. Leila and I would marry quietly with family only and save the rest. If the warehouse said no, I'd ask my uncle about his removals van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My heart's going a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move fast, not wait. Isn't that unusual for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Normally I wait to see. But if everyone's coming for the same warehouse jobs, the slow ones lose. My dad would say there's a time to be careful and a time to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd be thirty-one, married, maybe with a baby coming. I'd pray it's slower than they say.

say: I'd tell people to **keep their heads** and look after family.
I'd say get **hands-on work**, not handouts.
think: His desk job is **gone** almost at once.
Warehouse work lasts until **2031**, but everyone will compete for it.
do: Get the **forklift licence** that month and ask for nights.
Marry **quietly** with family only and save the rest.
Ask his uncle about the **removals van** if the warehouse says no.
S2.quote: If everyone's coming for the same warehouse jobs, the slow ones lose.
fieldNote: The short timeline makes this usually cautious man **move first**.
He frames family and **self-reliance** against government help.
He has **no plan** after the robots arrive in 2031.

steps.text: Take the forklift licence course that same month
Ask for warehouse nights, or removals work with his uncle
Marry quietly with family only and save the rest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still quick, but you can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if people stop complaining and get on with it. I'd tell the lads at work to get licences now. I'd say it at the mosque too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be off the customer line by 2029. The warehouse and driving last until about 2034. So I'd want to be in the warehouse, maybe driving a lorry, by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence this year and move to nights. Then I'd save for a lorry licence, which is about two thousand, because lorry drivers earn properly. Leila and I would get married next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. I know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand for a lorry licence on your savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night shifts pay a bit more, so I'd put that extra away for a year. My uncle might lend some, and I'd pay him back. Family helps family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI tools in the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the depot uses them for routes or stock, I'd learn them. I'm not against it, I just like to see it work first. In the warehouse, the scanners already tell you where everything goes.

say: I'd tell people to **get on with it** instead of complaining.
I'd urge the lads at work to get **licences** now.
think: He'd be off the customer line by about **2029**, once tracking calls are automated.
Warehouse and driving work last until about **2034**.
do: Get the **forklift licence** this year and move to nights.
Save about **two thousand** for a lorry licence.
feel: **Worried** but **steady**, because he knows what to do.
S3.quote: Night shifts pay a bit more, so I'd put that extra away for a year.
fieldNote: He plans a clear **ladder**: forklift, nights, then lorry.
He'd borrow from **family** rather than a bank.
With five years, the **wedding** stays on schedule.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence this year
Move to warehouse night shifts at the hub
Save two thousand from night pay for a lorry licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a fair bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare with that much warning. Young people should get a trade or a licence. Families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the customer line probably goes long before 2036. But ten years means I can do it step by step, warehouse first, then a lorry licence, then see. By 2039, when the robots come, I'd be thirty-nine and hopefully have some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the customer line for now and use the summary tool better. In a year I'd do the forklift licence, once more of the lads have. Leila and I would get married next summer and start saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A slow worry, not a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hopefully some savings. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard, on what we earn. But if I'm driving a lorry by thirty-two and Leila keeps her job, maybe. My parents saved on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with taking it step by step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm too slow and the good jobs go to quicker people. That's my weakness. I check everything twice, and I'd rather be careful than make a mess.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** not to prepare with that much warning.
I'd say young people need **a trade** and families should **plan together**.
think: The customer line probably goes **long before 2036**.
He can move **step by step** toward lorry driving before robots in 2039.
do: Stay on the customer line and use the **summary tool** better.
Take the **forklift licence** in a year, once more colleagues have.
Marry next summer and start saving for a **deposit**.
S4.quote: I check everything twice, and I'd rather be careful than make a mess.
fieldNote: With a decade, he goes back to his **careful** pace.
He names his own **slowness** as the main risk.
His parents' **saving habits** are his model.

steps.text: Use the tracking summary tool on every call

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because everyone would be fighting for the same warehouse jobs at once. What would help is apprenticeships and licences that companies pay for, so people can move into hands-on work. Not benefits, proper training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people in between. The office lads who aren't young enough to start fresh and aren't old enough to retire. I'm one of them, really.

headlineQuote: Everyone would be fighting for the same warehouse jobs at once.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** agent on a parcel firm's **customer line**, slow on claims because he checks every detail.
He lives with his partner, a **school receptionist**, and they're saving to marry without borrowing.
He is **traditional**, values self-reliance and family, and defends companies' right to change.
He uses AI **when it's proven** and plans a step-by-step move into the **warehouse** and driving.
Only the **two-year** picture makes him move first instead of waiting.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because everyone would compete for the same **warehouse jobs**.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid licences** and apprenticeships to move into hands-on work.
